newsitem.title: PHILIPPINES: Churches, karaoke bars yield no sign of "Mr Hwang".
newsitem.headline: Churches, karaoke bars yield no sign of "Mr Hwang".

text.p: The chase has led from churchmen to chambermaids, from diplomats to gardeners. A week after arriving in the Philippines, the man they call "Mr Hwang" has eluded detection, his movements clouded in mystery, his abode unknown.
Since a Chinese jetliner flew him into the country on Tuesday last week for a temporary asylum, North Korean defector Hwang Jang-yop and his guards have thrown all hunters off his scent.
One search yielded at least seven "Mr Hwangs" or "Mr Wangs" on an airline list. Another plane turned up a Taiwanese monk.
One trail led to a karaoke bar in the northern mountain city of Baguio -- but the "Mr Hwang" whom a bar girl said bought her rounds of drinks nights earlier was not the one.
"Maybe you are not looking hard enough," Philippine armed forces intelligence chief Major-General Benjamin Libarnes said.

Libarnes, the Filipino general in charge of protecting Pyongyang's top ideologue from assassins, said Hwang was in a safe sanctuary somewhere in the country, watching cable television and eating dishes prepared by a special cook.
Pyongyang's top idealogue, who defected to the South Korean mission in Beijing last February 12, was whisked off to the Philippines a month later.

Since his arrival, dozens of Filipino, Japanese and South Korean reporters and television crewmen have mounted stakeouts in Baguio where Hwang was initially thought to have been taken after his arrival at the former U.S. Clark airbase near Manila.
"The last guest we had here was President (Fidel) Ramos," a gardener at Baguio's presidential summer mansion told Reuters.
A chambermaid swore she saw no one that morning when she dusted up the mansion's six-room guest house.
Filipino, South Korean and American diplomats said they did not know the defector's whereabouts.
The hunt has also led reporters to a South Korean church, but it was closed and neighbours said they had not noticed anything unusual at the place.
Checks of hotel registries, a logbook at a U.S. diplomatic compound and a country club failed to yield any trace of the most hunted foreign visitor the Philippines has ever had.
"Few secrets are kept in this open society," Amando Doronila, political analyst of the Philippine Daily Inquirer newspaper, said in a commentary on Sunday.
Hwang's whereabouts "is one of the best kept secrets this country has ever had, given its reputation for leakages of classified information," Doronila added.
At least half a dozen airports are under close media watch, in case Hwang is moved to another hideout or flown out to Seoul.
A private jet that landed at Clark one afternoon and disgorged Oriental-looking men set off a scramble among TV cameramen and photographers.
The Orientals turned out to be Taiwanese businessmen flying in to try their luck at a casino at nearby Subic Bay freeport.
Three men, one of whom wore the habit of monk and also looked like an Oriental, started a similar scramble in Baguio.
Asked if he was Mr Hwang, the monk said: "No, I am Mr. Wong."
